articles.title: ‘Rio,’ ‘Ice Age’ Director Carlos Saldanha on ‘Wonderful Homecoming’ With Ambitious Brazilian Adventure Film ‘100 Days’: ‘It Deserved a Big Cinema Treatment’
articles.summary: It might have taken pioneering explorer Amyr Klink one hundred days to cross the Atlantic, but it took Carlos Saldanha almost three thousand to bring his story to the big screen.
body: Once he boarded the project, Saldanha reworked the script alongside Elena Soarez and Thais Tavares. The pandemic years slowed the project’s development, but granted the creative team more time to finesse the details of the adaptation. “To me, it wasn’t enough to just tell the tale of this hundred-day adventure,” says the director. “I was very interested in what was going on in Amyr’s head, what he did while he spent such a long time rowing all by himself, all alone in the sea.”

“I talked a lot with Amyr, with his family and friends, and did very in-depth research to understand who this person was and what moved him,” he adds. “Amyr was great in how much freedom he granted us. He helped us decipher him without having to spell it out for us.”

articles.summary: Following major openings like “Obsession,” “Backrooms” and “Resident Evil,” the horror genre’s 2026 box office reign shows no sign of slowing. And with Halloween right around the corner, it makes sense that momentum continued Friday as the supernatural, unnerving thriller “Other Mommy” easily…
body: Fellow new release “ The Social Reckoning ” landed in fourth place on Friday with $2.15 million from 2,606 North American theaters. The movie is expected to make $6 million domestically through the weekend.

Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to 2010’s “The Social Network” (which grossed $224 million globally and went on to win four Oscars), the corporate drama has been afflicted with mixed reviews since its premiere earlier this week; Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “a diverting-enough, clever-enough, true-enough examination” that serves as “a reminder that ‘The Social Network’ was both Sorkin’s best writing achievement and… his least characteristic.”

“The Social Reckoning” follows Facebook’s 2021 leak by whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison). Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg and Jeremy Allen White plays Jeff Horwitz, the Wall Street Journal reporter who digs through thousands of pages of internal documents, which culminated in his Pulitzer Prize-winning reporting, “The Facebook Files.” Bill Burr, Betty Gilpin and Billy Magnussen also star.

articles.title: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US
articles.summary: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen. On 20 January 2025, with 14 minutes remaining in his term as president, Joe Biden commuted the life sentence of Leonard Peltier, after…
body: Outside the Florida prison where Peltier was being held that morning were several of the many activists and lawyers who fought for his release, as well as film-makers David France and Jesse Short Bull. The two directors’ long-gestating documentary on Peltier’s fight for justice was set to premiere just a week later at the Sundance film festival with a very different ending, the octogenarian still awaiting a chance to return home to the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa reservation in North Dakota. That morning, there was “a sinking feeling that it wasn’t going to happen”, France said.

When it did, while the cameras rolled, the line of supporters erupted in joy for a commutation that allowed Peltier to serve the rest of his consecutive life sentences on house arrest, though it did not pardon him – not quite justice, but a victory so uncertain and so hard-fought, over more than half a lifetime, that I have cried every time I’ve rewatched it.

As director Brad Bird noted in the introduction at the Royal Festival Hall, the premiere for the neo-noir sci-fi was also composer Michael…
body: “I really was so excited to work with Brad, I’m such a massive fan of his,” she said. “It was a dream of mine to collaborate with him on anything — I just wanted to work with him so badly.”
Johansson voices Venus Nova, a famous pop star and love interest to Rockwell’s Raymond “Ray” Gunn, a small-time private detective.

”And, of course, [Bird] had written all his characters as very complex,” she added. “I’ve worked with directors that direct animated movies, but it was such a different experience working with Brad on this because he’s coming at it from also this other artistic perspective.”
Asked about the inspiration for the film, Bird said that it came “idiotically after misunderstanding a song,” the B-52’s sci-fi inspired 1979 track “Planet Claire.”

articles.title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Breakout Portia Doubleday on Playing ‘White Girl Wasted’ Conspiracy Theorist: ‘I Knew People Who Were Radicalized’
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “The Social Reckoning,” now playing in theaters. Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning” begins with a vignette about the impact of social media that’s as chilling as any statistic about the dangers of social media.
body: This interaction, one that will feel unfortunately familiar to any viewer who’s spent time online this decade, sits at the heart of “The Social Reckoning.” Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” the 2010 film he wrote about the earliest days of Facebook, “Reckoning” confronts the world Mark Zuckerberg has brought into being.

Kaylee is a person whose particular brand of rage could only exist in a post-social media world. After all, we learn she’s something of a changeling: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) knew Kaylee as a bleeding-heart leftist. By the film’s end, Frances has been so moved by Kaylee’s trajectory that she decides to spill the secrets of Facebook’s indifference to the harm it causes. Kaylee, meanwhile, joins the Jan. 6 insurrection.

Doubleday may be best known for her work on USA’s Emmy-winning drama “Mr. Robot,” in which she played a conflicted employee at the series’ central villainous tech concern, E Corp. As she tells Variety, on the week of “The Social Reckoning’s” release, the way technology affects our cognition is a live concern for her, and has had direct consequences in her own life.

articles.title: Ray Gunn review – Brad Bird’s animated film-noir sci-fi caper is an old-school family classic
articles.summary: Sam Rockwell voices the gumshoe who becomes embroiled with Scarlett Johansson’s femme fatale in this big-hearted and beautifully designed fantasy spectacular. Brad Bird, the Spielberg of animation, applies his masterly authorial touch to a terrific family film that retrieves the genre from the…
body: When Venus discovers his planned scam, she threatens to kill Arnold in front of witnesses, creating a murderous cloud over her reputation – but malevolent Arnold has something on her too. It all leads to a scary plot, involving Venus’s smoothie manager and first husband Barry (Alan Tudyk) and fez-wearing nightclub proprietor and mob boss Slugsy (Matt Berry), who comes on like a cross between Sydney Greenstreet and Jabba the Hutt.

There are some lovely set piece scenes – especially when Ray and Venus take to the floor at a club which offers a “zero gravity” interlude allowing its dancers and lovers the chance to float surreally around as if in space. We also get a bizarre interlude when a gun turns out to be – temporarily – capable of scrambling the limbs of those in its sights. And on top of all that, the film has something to say about algorithmic ads and data privacy. It’s a charming, very enjoyable movie with a big heart.

articles.title: 10 Best Western Movies Of The 2000s, Ranked
articles.summary: The Western genre may not be thriving as much as it did decades ago, but the 2000s gave us plenty of outstanding movies in the genre worth watching.
body: The Western experienced a slow decline throughout the 1990s, from being by far the biggest entertainment genre in the early days of film and television — with exponentially more Westerns made from the 1930s through the 1950s than any other genre — to a trickle of more revisionist or subversive versions that countered the fact that the genre's traditional forms were rooted in classical ideas that had become old-fashioned. As the world advanced, it constantly threatened to outdate the Western.

However, the genre could never truly die, as it's far too rooted in elemental ideas about the creation of America. By the 2000s, Western films were certainly in a low period in terms of output, but the decade produced some of the best films the genre has ever seen. Just as the 21st century as a whole can't be counted out when it comes to Westerns — as seen in our list of the 15 best Western movies of the 21st century — the aughts have substance to spare in their depictions of the mythic stories we tell ourselves about America.

articles.title: The Social Reckoning's Failure Can Be Traced Back To One Moment
articles.summary: Most folks agree that The Social Reckoning doesn't come close to living up to The Social Network, and we can pinpoint where the trouble began.
body: The second that Jesse Eisenberg declined to join "The Social Reckoning," the standalone sequel to "The Social Network" that brings screenwriter Aaron Sorkin back but also tasks him with pulling double duty as director, the project should have been abandoned. Sadly, it went ahead as planned, and we got... "The Social Reckoning," which replaces Eisenberg as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg with "Succession" veteran Jeremy Strong and which, incidentally, is a bad movie.

I'm on record right here at /Film explaining precisely why "The Social Reckoning" doesn't even deserve to be mentioned in the same breath as "The Social Network," and when it comes to the recasting of Zuckerberg, it's one of the film's many, many glaring problems. Sure, I get that Eisenberg chose not to revisit this role, which scored him his first Oscar nomination over a decade ago, for a whole host of reasons. But, truthfully, "The Social Reckoning" failed before it started by bringing Strong in to portray the Facebook creator.

articles.title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Sam Rockwell and Scarlett Johansson in Brad Bird’s Forgettable Netflix Animated Neo-Noir
articles.summary: Produced by Skydance Animation's John Lasseter and also starring Tom Waits and Bobby Cannavale, the film follows a golden-hearted private eye hired to wrangle a famously volatile starlet.
body: Ray Gunn ( Sam Rockwell ), private eye, is special. He’s “the only honest player in a crooked game,” the only dick who prioritizes things like truth and justice over cold hard cash. In a retrofuturistic society where aliens are disdained as second-class citizens, he’s the rare human who stands up for extraterrestrials. Some scorn him for his heroism; others admire him for it; all agree he’s something of an oddity.

The screenplay, by Bird and Matthew Robbins, assembles paper-thin characters in service of a PG storyline that’s simultaneously too simplistic for adults and too serious-minded for kids. In the bustling city of Metropia — think 1940s Manhattan but with hovercars and jetpacks — Ray is a detective so hard up for cash that his office gets a little emptier every time he returns to it, his coat rack and his couch and then his desk getting repo’d one by one.
